summary:
Allwork.space profiles five coworking and flexible workspace markets it considers notable in 2026, arguing that flex space now spans private offices, enterprise suites, meeting rooms and managed offices used by companies of all sizes rather than just freelance day desks.

India is presented as the clearest case of flex becoming a corporate real estate strategy. The sector passed 100 million square feet in 2026, driven by enterprise demand, longer contracts and managed workspace adoption. In Q2 2026 flex providers were the country's largest office occupiers at 27% of gross office leasing, ahead of tech (21%) and BFSI (13%). Delhi-NCR saw flex operators take 45% of regional office transactions, a record quarterly share, followed by Pune (38%), Bengaluru (26%) and Hyderabad (24%). First-half 2026 coworking leasing hit a record 8.6 million square feet across the seven largest markets, up 32% year over year (Colliers India via Outlook Business), with Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR and Hyderabad making up nearly two-thirds. National operators such as WeWork India, Awfis, Smartworks, 91Springboard and Innov8 command 19% higher pricing than independents, reflecting a premium for standardized, multi-city experience.

Kenya is framed as a mobility-driven growth market: Nairobi's startup ecosystem plus a new digital nomad permit pathway for foreign remote workers, with IWG planning to double its Kenyan locations.

Singapore is described as Asia's premium market, with flex demand up 5% year over year last year and inquiries up 37% quarter over quarter in early 2025, plus pricing premiums for higher-end space, driven by multinationals and regional headquarters.

The United States remains the largest market, reaching 9,136 locations and 163.9 million square feet by the end of Q1 2026, with growth spreading into mid-sized markets alongside innovation hubs including San Francisco, New York, Boston, Austin, Seattle and Chicago. The U.K. and Ireland section is truncated but positioned as an example of mature flex.
